title: AARO's historical record reports and their critics
notes: Start-here flag 4. It sits on most shortest paths between the board's regions, so it must be a topic, not a shortcut.

lead.text: Volume I of AARO's Historical Record Report, released on 8 March 2024, concludes that there is no empirical evidence that the US government and private companies have been reverse-engineering extraterrestrial technology. The Volume II it promised, owed under the same statutory requirement, had not been published as of August 2026.

summary.text: The report comes from sec. 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA, which requires the Director of the Office to submit within 540 days a written report on the government's historical record on UAP from 1 January 1945, itemising among other things restricted-access programmes not clearly reported to Congress and any efforts to hide or manipulate public opinion about UAP.

Volume I is dated February 2024, was cleared for open publication by DOPSR on 6 March 2024 and runs to 63 pages. It was prepared under Kirkpatrick's direction and released after he left, with Acting Director Tim Phillips fronting the rollout and media engagement.

By its own account AARO reviewed every official investigatory effort since 1945, searched classified and unclassified archives, conducted about 30 interviews and worked with the officials who oversee controlled and special access programmes. Among the efforts it catalogues is NASA's UAP Independent Study Team.

Volume I defers its unresolved allegations to a Volume II covering research from 1 November 2023 to 15 April 2024. That second volume is the outstanding half of the statutory requirement, and it is where the Department said it would publish its Yankee Blue findings.

record.text: Volume I states that AARO found no empirical evidence of reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial technology, and no evidence that any government investigation, academic research or official panel has confirmed that any UAP sighting was extraterrestrial technology. It attributes the modern claims largely to circular reporting among a consistent group of individuals active since 2009.

The report says none of its interviewees had firsthand knowledge of the programmes they described, and that most claims were inaccurate or misidentified authentic classified programmes unrelated to UAP.

Among the interviewee claims it records are a thirdhand account that an organisation held twelve spacecraft recovered before 1970, some intact, in a CIA partnership that ended in 1989, and a senior military officer's description of a craft floating in a building with about 150 people working on the programme outside government.

Its section on named sensitive programmes discloses three: KONA BLUE, a prospective DHS special access programme rejected by DHS leadership for lacking merit; the Virtual Institute for Satellite Integration Training, which it says was a private UAP organisation's project that NASA did not sponsor; and an unnamed intelligence community controlled access programme expanded in 2021 to include a UAP reverse-engineering mission and later disestablished.

On KONA BLUE the report states that Senators Lieberman and Reid asked for the programme to be established, that it traces its origins to the DIA-managed AAWSAP/AATIP programme, and that no extraterrestrial craft or bodies were ever collected: the material was only assumed to exist by its advocates.

The report confirms the $22 million appropriated at Senator Reid's direction for DIA in the FY2008 and FY2010 Defense Appropriations Acts, that DIA established AAWSAP in 2009, the contractor's UFO research, the Utah property investigation, and a 2012 termination.

Volume I names no private individuals, referring only to the private sector organisation, the DIA programme manager and the head of the organisation. A full-text search finds no occurrence of Wilson or Davis, and no mention of Kirtland, AFOSI, Bennewitz, Doty, MJ-12, Rendlesham or the Wilson-Davis notes.

The report concludes that the Roswell materials were consistent with a Project Mogul balloon, and that a sample offered as extraterrestrial was a manufactured terrestrial alloy of magnesium, zinc and bismuth.

AARO says it reviewed programmes through a partnership with the special access programme control offices of DoD, the intelligence community and DHS, with full access to all pertinent programmes. Its corporate findings rest on executives and chief technology officers of the named companies denying the programmes on the record; the report describes no inspection of any contractor facility.

Volume I says AARO found no non-disclosure agreements containing UAP information, and lists among its future lines of effort engaging with the named companies alleged to have worked with the government on UAP recovery.

The statutory deadline for the historical report was 15 June 2024. As of 12 August 2026 no Volume II appears in AARO's index of congressional products or on the Department of War's release index, and the FY2024 report mentions only Volume I.

claimed.text: Officials have repeatedly promised Volume II: Pentagon spokesman Pat Ryder said in August 2024 the review was continuing with nothing to announce on timing, Kosloski told reporters in November 2024 it would come within months, and a DoD spokeswoman told the Wall Street Journal in June 2025 that it would carry the Yankee Blue findings and was scheduled for late 2025.

According to the Wall Street Journal's reporting, AARO discovered the Yankee Blue practice during Kirkpatrick's tenure, and officials briefed DNI Haines that hundreds of military personnel had been affected over decades by a fake alien-technology indoctrination.

Kirkpatrick, who directed Volume I, argued in Scientific American seven weeks after leaving AARO that the crash-retrieval narrative is circular reporting traceable to Robert Bigelow and AATIP, and that the allegations come from inadvertent disclosure of legitimate programmes or from unsupported belief.

James Lacatski hinted in April 2026 that a smaller, more focused effort related to the proposed KONA BLUE programme continued after AAWSAP ended, which would cut against Volume I's account that the proposal went nowhere.

contested.text: Volume I's statement that AARO found no UAP-related non-disclosure agreements cannot stand beside the Department's later confirmation that Air Force personnel signed NDAs over a fictitious alien-technology programme. The board infers that such a practice falls inside the statute's clause on efforts to hide or manipulate information, yet no account of it appears in Volume I.

The widely repeated claim that AARO acknowledged Yankee Blue in Volume I does not survive a full-text check, and was asserted on this board until 12 August 2026. The Yankee Blue account itself remains unanchored: a Pentagon spokesperson could not confirm the memo described in the press, and Greenewald's FOIA requests returned no records before an appeal was granted and remanded.
Deputy Secretary Hicks declined to publicly endorse the report's key findings, and Christopher Mellon called them mid-level assertions lacking cabinet-level ratification.

The board reads the report as confirming the money, the programme, the contractor work and the attempted DHS transfer while withholding every name, which makes it citable but not actionable for oversight, and as treating Elizondo's claimed role as outside the record rather than rebutting it.

On the board's inference, AARO's lack-of-merit framing of AAWSAP is contradicted by DIA's own 2009 quality review, which found the reviews positive, and a KONA BLUE proposal to protect recovered biologics presupposes the holdings AARO says were only assumed to exist.

The board infers that the report does not address the 1995 GAO finding that Roswell-era base records were destroyed without authority, nor the Bolender memorandum's statement that national-security UFO reports sat outside Blue Book.

The board infers that the statute requires one historical report, so the split into volumes is AARO's own construction and the requirement has been only partly met since 15 June 2024; and that five tranches of raw imagery clearing in three months, against a narrative volume withheld for two years, shows the bottleneck is analytic conclusions rather than sources and methods.

The board reads Kirkpatrick's op-ed as a rollout technique that previewed the report's conclusions before publication, and notes that his circular-reporting thesis was right in form but, on the Yankee Blue record, wrong about who seeded the belief.

questions: Why has Volume II not been published, who decided to defer it, and does a draft exist?
Which companies did AARO visit, and did it ever inspect a contractor facility rather than accept executives' statements?
Was AARO given access to waived or unacknowledged special access programmes, or only to those the control offices chose to show it?
Does the department-level memo on Yankee Blue exist, and when was DNI Haines briefed on it?
Why does a report written under a statute requiring an account of efforts to hide UAP information say nothing about Kirtland, AFOSI or the Wilson-Davis notes?
